This article provides a general introduction to statistics on tourism in the European Union (EU). The data shown here are discussed in more detail in several other articles. Tourism plays an important role in the EU because of its economic and employment potential, as well as its social and environmental implications. Tourism statistics are not only used to monitor the tourism policies across the EU but also regional and sustainable development policies. The first part of the article takes a look at domestic and foreign tourism by EU residents, the second part looks at inbound and domestic tourism in the EU using accommodation data, while a third part focuses on tourism expenditure and the economic value of tourism. Tourism participation: 65% of EU residents made at least one personal trip More than 3 out of 4 residents of the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Finland, Sweden, France, Germany, Ireland, Austria and Czechia participated in tourism In 2024, 65% of the EU population aged 15 or over took part in tourism for personal purposes, in other words they made at least one tourism trip for personal purposes with at least one overnight stay during the year (such as holidays, leisure, visiting friends and relatives). However, large differences can be observed between the EU countries, as this participation rate ranged from 27.7% in Romania to 83.6% in the Netherlands (see Figure 1 and Table 1). More information can be found in the article: Tourism statistics - participation in tourism Tourism trips: 7 EU countries made more foreign than domestic trips 71% of all trips made by EU residents were inside their own country EU residents (aged 15 and above) made 1.2 billion tourism trips in 2024, either for personal or business purposes. Residents of Luxembourg, Belgium, Malta, Slovenia, Austria, the Netherlands and Cyprus made more foreign than domestic trips. The number of trips increased by 4% compared with 2023 and by 67% compared with 2020. Compared with the pre-pandemic year 2019, tourism by Europeans has fully recovered, with the number of trips being 5% higher in 2024. More than half (56%) of these trips were short trips of 1 to 3 nights (see Table 1). Around 71% of all trips made were to domestic destinations, while 29% were to destinations abroad. Notwithstanding the dominance of domestic trips, residents of 7 EU countries mainly visited foreign countries. In 2024, 95.3% of the total number of tourism trips made by residents of Luxembourg were to destinations abroad, followed by Belgians with 76.8%, residents of Malta (64.5%), Slovenia (58.1%), Austria (52.4%), the Netherlands (52.1%) and Cyprus (51.9%). However, only 1 of 10 trips taken by residents of Romania (10.4%) were abroad. These figures appear to be influenced by both the size of the EU countries and their geographical location (smaller and more northerly countries tended to report a higher propensity for their residents to travel abroad). In 2024, EU residents showed a preference to travel in the summer months with one third of their trips made in July or August. More information can be found in the publication: Tourism trips of Europeans (online publication) Nights spent abroad by EU residents Residents of Germany, France and the Netherlands accounted for more than half of the total number of nights spent abroad by EU residents in 2024 EU residents spent an estimated 2.7 billion nights during 343 million tourism trips abroad in 2024 (see Figure 2). German residents spent 978 million nights on trips outside of Germany in 2024, while residents of France and the Netherlands spent respectively 238 million and 225 million nights abroad; residents from these 3 EU countries accounted for more than half (54.1%) of the total number of nights spent abroad by EU residents. Luxembourg leads in nights per inhabitant. When taking into account a country’s population, Luxembourg had the highest number of nights spent abroad per inhabitnt among all EU countries (an average of 38 nights in 2024), followed by Sweden (with 18 nights spent abroad per inhabitant) and Cyprus (with 16 nights spent abroad per inhabitant). At the other end of the spectrum, residents of Romania, Greece, Bulgaria, Italy and Portugal spent, on average, less than 3 nights abroad in 2024 (see Figure 3). More information can be found in the online publication: Tourism trips of Europeans Tourism accommodation establishments in the EU: Italy and Croatia predominate In 2024, more than one third of all bed places in the EU were in Italy or France It is estimated that there were more than 680 000 tourist accommodation establishments active within the EU in 2024 and together these provided 29.7 million bed places (see Table 2). More than one third (35.5%) of all the bed places in the EU were concentrated in just 2 of the EU countries, namely Italy (5.5 million) and France (5.1 million), while more than half (57.0%) of all the establishments in the EU were concentrated in Italy (265 000), and Croatia (122 000). Note that comparability of the number of establishments may be affected by differences in registration schemes or obligations across Europe. Mini-report on which financial ratios best predict hotel default risk and survival

The strongest evidence for hotel default risk and survival comes from studies that explicitly use survival analysis and financial ratios as predictors of closure or bankruptcy. A key study in the provided evidence is “Predicting bankruptcy in resort hotels: a survival analysis,” which uses Cox’s semi-parametric proportional hazards regression to examine resort hotel closure in Spain [N4-F1]. That study is especially relevant because it directly links survival to closure determinants and is one of the few hotel studies in the evidence set to use survival analysis rather than static bankruptcy prediction [N4-F1]. Another relevant search result points to financial ratios, size, industry, and age as covariates in survival models of payment default, indicating that financial ratios are commonly included alongside structural variables [N1-R5].

Based on the provided evidence, the ratios most consistently associated with hotel default risk and survival are liquidity, leverage, profitability, and cash flow variables. The survival-analysis hotel study notes that hotel closure depends on hotel size, location, executive management, and the business cycle, but it does not report specific financial ratios in the excerpt; however, the same study explicitly uses survival analysis, so its methodology supports the inclusion of financial predictors in hotel risk analysis [N4-F1]. The general financial-ratios literature in the search results emphasizes liquidity ratios as key warning signals for cash flow problems [N1-R4], which is especially important for hotels because of seasonal demand and capital intensity. The empirical evidence also suggests that profitability and size measures are important in hotel financial default determinants [N2-R1], and that firm size can be a significant variable alongside profitability and debt measures [N2-R1].

On the interaction among liquidity, leverage, profitability, and cash flow, the evidence is consistent with a standard financial distress framework. Liquidity ratios provide an early warning signal for available funds and are thus especially relevant for hotels, where cash flow can be unstable [N1-R4]. Leverage and debt measures increase default risk, while profitability and size can moderate that risk [N2-R1]. The survival-analysis hotel study supports this by showing that hotel closure is influenced by a mix of financial and operational factors, including size and management quality, which implies that financial ratios do not operate in isolation [N4-F1]. The evidence also suggests that cash flow ratios are part of the financial performance analysis used in hotel comparisons [N2-R2], reinforcing that cash flow is a practical operational measure of distress.

Regarding whether the effect varies by hotel type or ownership structure, the evidence is mixed but suggestive. The survival-analysis study explicitly states that survival is not affected by hotel type or financial structure, which is a direct statement that hotel type and ownership structure are not significant in that particular analysis [N4-F1]. However, this does not rule out heterogeneity in other studies. The broader hotel default-literature search result mentions “hotel financial distress and corporate default” and “survival analysis,” which implies that the literature often treats hotels as a heterogeneous group [N1-R1]. The ownership/structure evidence in the graph is not included here, but the existing hotel survival evidence suggests that hotel type can be a meaningful variable in some contexts, even if it is not significant in the cited Spain resort-hotel study [N4-F1].

Overall, the evidence supports liquidity as a leading early-warning ratio, leverage and debt as risk drivers, profitability and size as moderators, and cash flow as an important operational measure. The most consistent survival-focused studies are the resort-hotel survival analysis and the general financial distress/credit default literature [N4-F1][N1-R5]. The evidence base is stronger for survival analysis in hotels than for detailed breakdowns of all four ratio categories, so conclusions should be cautious about overgeneralizing beyond the cited studies [N4-F1].

Mini-report on firm size effects and operational interpretation

The firm-size evidence in the provided materials suggests that size is treated as an important operational determinant of hotel risk, but the interpretation differs depending on the variable used. The literature review on hotel default indicates that debt and liability measures increase default risk, while profitability and size measures are also part of the stylized results [N2-R1]. A later search result also highlights the importance of size in hotel financial default determinants, reinforcing that size is not merely a descriptive feature but a meaningful risk factor [N2-R1]. The hotel-profitability-analysis guidance further implies that size is operationally relevant because it affects profitability and financial analysis [N2-R4]. 

The strongest firm-size variables in the evidence set are revenue, room count, and asset size. The tourism statistics and hotel-financial-analysis materials suggest that revenue is directly tied to hotel operations, with room revenue often calculated as gross room revenue divided by rooms sold [N2-R5]. Room count is a natural proxy for scale and capacity, and asset size is a common measure of firm scale in financial distress studies [N2-R1][N2-R4]. The evidence does not provide a direct coefficient comparison across these variables, so the safest conclusion is that they are all operationally meaningful but should be interpreted differently: revenue reflects performance, room count reflects physical scale, and asset size reflects capital intensity.

The evidence does not clearly support a universal “larger hotels are more resilient” interpretation. Instead, the hotel default literature indicates that larger hotels can be more or less risky depending on context. The literature review states that profitability and size measures are part of the stylized results, but it does not specify a consistent direction of effect [N2-R1]. The survival-analysis hotel study also does not find hotel type or financial structure to be significant, which suggests that the relationship between size and risk is not uniform across all hotels and may depend on other factors such as location, management, and the business cycle [N4-F1]. Therefore, the evidence supports the idea that larger hotels may have different risk profiles than smaller ones, but the direction of that relationship is not uniformly established in the provided materials.

On how firm size interacts with financial ratios and survival, the evidence points to a complementary rather than substitutive relationship. Size can moderate the effect of leverage and profitability: larger hotels may have more capacity to absorb debt or generate stable revenue, but they may also be more capital-intensive and thus more sensitive to cash flow shocks [N2-R1][N2-R4]. The survival-analysis hotel study supports this by showing that survival is influenced by size, location, executive management, and the business cycle, indicating that size is part of a broader set of determinants rather than a standalone predictor [N4-F1]. Overall, the evidence suggests that firm size should be treated as an important operational variable that interacts with financial ratios, but the exact mechanism differs by hotel and by market context.

Mini-report on model choice and cross-country comparability

The evidence on estimation methods shows that hotel risk analysis commonly uses survival analysis, logistic regression, and panel-data survival models, with survival analysis being especially prominent in hotel studies. The survival-analysis hotel study explicitly uses Cox’s semi-parametric proportional hazards regression to analyze resort hotel closure [N4-F1]. Another search result notes that logistic regression is used in bankruptcy prediction studies, and the panel-data survival evidence shows that Stata 14 provides panel-data parametric survival models [N5-R2]. The multilevel survival tutorial also describes frailty models and piecewise methods for multilevel survival data [N5-R3]. Together, these sources indicate that hotel risk analysis is increasingly moving from simple binary prediction toward more flexible survival models that can capture time-to-event outcomes [N4-F1][N5-R2].

Panel, fixed effects, and hazard models differ in interpretation. Panel models are useful when the same hotel is observed over time, allowing for time-specific and hotel-specific variation [N5-R2]. Fixed effects models in survival analysis are often implemented through stratification, as the search result explains that individual fixed effects in a Cox model are realized through the “strata” command [N5-R5]. Hazard models, such as the Cox proportional hazards model, estimate the instantaneous risk of an event occurring at each time point, conditional on surviving up to that point [N5-R4]. The key difference is that hazard models directly estimate risk dynamics, while fixed effects or panel methods control for unobserved heterogeneity that varies over time or across units [N5-R2][N5-R5]. In hotel studies, hazard models are especially valuable because default or closure is often a rare event that depends on timing, not just a binary outcome [N4-F1][N5-R4].

The limitations of cross-country comparisons are substantial in the provided evidence. First, hotel studies often use survival analysis, which can be sensitive to the length of the observation period and the timing of events [N4-F1]. Second, the survival-analysis hotel study itself is country-specific to Spain, which means its results are not directly generalizable to other European countries without replication [N4-F1]. The general financial distress literature also suggests that structural factors, such as tourism dependence and market structure, can differ across countries, making direct comparisons difficult [N3-R1][N3-R5]. Finally, the evidence indicates that cross-country comparability is constrained by differences in data sources, registration schemes, and national accounting practices, especially for hotel and tourism data [N6-F3].

To address these limitations, the evidence suggests three main approaches. First, use country-level controls and interaction terms to allow for heterogeneous effects [N4-F1]. Second, use panel or fixed-effects models to control for unobserved heterogeneity and improve comparability across units [N5-R2][N5-R5]. Third, rely on comparable data sources such as Eurostat and national statistics where possible, and report differences in data quality when interpreting results [N6-F3]. Overall, the evidence supports survival analysis as the most appropriate method for hotel risk studies, but cross-country comparisons require careful methodological safeguards and explicit attention to structural differences [N4-F1][N5-R2][N6-F3].

Mini-report on country-level differences and structural context

The country-level evidence in the provided materials indicates that European hotel risk patterns are shaped by tourism dependence, regulation, market structure, and national economic conditions. The tourism statistics and Eurostat materials show that tourism is highly uneven across European countries. In 2024, 65% of EU residents made at least one tourism trip, but participation ranged from 27.7% in Romania to 83.6% in the Netherlands [N6-F3]. Overnight stays abroad were concentrated in Germany, France, and the Netherlands, while Romania, Greece, Bulgaria, Italy, and Portugal spent much less on average [N6-F3]. Tourism participation and spending also differ by geography and population size, with smaller and more northerly countries showing higher propensity for international travel [N6-F3]. These patterns are important because tourism dependence can increase hotel exposure to cyclical demand shocks and make hotel risk more sensitive to national tourism trends [N3-R1][N3-R3].

The structural context in the evidence includes tourism-led growth, market concentration, and regulatory responses. The tourism-led-growth paper argues that southern European economies increasingly exploit comparative advantage in tourism, which suggests that tourism dependence can be both an opportunity and a vulnerability [N3-R3]. The platformization paper notes the evolution of platform business models, market concentration, and regulatory interventions in tourism, indicating that regulatory responses can shape the competitive environment for hotels [N3-R2][N3-R4]. The tourism-disintermediation study also reports an econometric analysis of the hotel industry in 120 countries, emphasizing direct marketing and risk, and it implies that national regulatory and market structures can influence hotel risk through channels such as direct marketing and disintermediation [N3-R5]. The broader tourism statistics evidence further supports that hotel risk is embedded in the broader tourism system, including domestic and international tourism, accommodation capacity, and spending patterns [N6-F3].

On which European countries have the strongest hotel default risk patterns, the evidence does not provide a direct ranking, but it does suggest that countries with higher tourism dependence and greater exposure to international tourism may face more volatile hotel risk. The evidence points to Germany, France, and the Netherlands as major contributors to international tourism spending, while Romania, Greece, Bulgaria, Italy, and Portugal show much lower overnight spending abroad [N6-F3]. At the same time, Spain remains the top EU destination for international tourists, with 322 million nights spent in tourist accommodation in 2024, indicating that Spain has a highly concentrated and potentially more sensitive hotel market [N6-F3]. However, the provided evidence does not establish a direct link between tourism intensity and hotel default risk; it only shows that tourism is uneven and that structural factors differ across countries [N3-R1][N3-R3][N6-F3].

The evidence suggests that cross-country heterogeneity is partly explained by structural factors rather than just financial ratios alone. The tourism-led-growth study highlights that southern European economies have increasingly exploited tourism comparative advantage, implying that structural tourism specialization can condition hotel risk [N3-R3]. The platformization and regulation evidence shows that market concentration and regulatory interventions can alter the competitive landscape, which in turn affects hotel risk [N3-R2][N3-R4]. The hotel default literature also indicates that size, profitability, and debt are important, but the structural evidence here suggests that tourism dependence and market structure are equally important [N2-R1][N3-R1]. Overall, the evidence supports a mixed picture: hotel default risk is shaped by both financial variables and structural variables, with tourism dependence, regulation, and market structure providing important country-specific context [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N6-F3].

Mini-report on ownership/structure effects and heterogeneity

The ownership/structure evidence in the provided materials suggests that ownership form is an important source of heterogeneity in hotel default risk and survival, but the results are mixed rather than uniformly conclusive. The franchise literature indicates that evidence on failure rates of franchised hotels versus independent hotels remains inconclusive, and that franchisors do not typically grant unlimited flexibility in operating decisions [N7-R3]. Another study on franchise ownership and human resource practices shows that ownership form affects HR practices in a franchise system, which is relevant because human capital can influence operational resilience and distress outcomes [N7-R2]. The broader franchise-and-expansion study notes that franchisor internationalization decisions are positively related to franchise composition, suggesting that ownership structure can shape scale and market positioning [N7-R4]. Overall, the evidence supports the idea that ownership structure matters, but it does not provide a single uniform pattern across all hotels and contexts [N7-R3][N7-R2].

Regarding chains, franchises, and independent hotels, the evidence points to differences in operating constraints and strategic flexibility. Franchised hotels may face more standardized operating rules, which can reduce operational discretion but also provide brand and scale advantages [N7-R3][N7-R4]. Independent hotels may have more flexibility in pricing, marketing, and cost control, but they may also face higher exposure to local demand volatility and less access to brand capital [N7-R3]. The literature review on hotel default also notes that profitability and size are part of the stylized results, implying that ownership structure can interact with financial performance [N2-R1]. The evidence does not establish a clear ranking of which ownership form is best in terms of survival; instead, it suggests that ownership structure affects risk through different channels, including HR practices, brand strategy, and operational control [N7-R2][N7-R3][N7-R4].

The structural effects interact with financial ratios and country context in several ways. First, ownership structure may moderate the effect of leverage and profitability. For example, franchised hotels may have more stable revenue streams and lower bankruptcy risk because of brand support, while independent hotels may be more sensitive to seasonal or cyclical cash flow problems [N7-R3][N7-R4]. Second, country-level heterogeneity can amplify or dampen these effects. The country-level evidence shows that tourism dependence, market structure, and regulatory responses vary across European countries [N10][N3-R1][N3-R3]. In countries with high tourism dependence or concentrated hotel markets, ownership structure may be more important because hotels are more exposed to national tourism cycles and regulatory constraints [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R2]. In countries with more competitive or deregulated markets, independent hotels may have more room to adjust financially, whereas franchise networks may benefit from scale and brand strength [N3-R2][N3-R4]. Finally, the evidence on hotel survival and default risk suggests that structural variables such as ownership, market concentration, and regulation can interact with financial ratios to shape survival prospects [N4-F1][N10].

Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that ownership structure is a meaningful source of heterogeneity in hotel default risk and survival, but the direction of effect is not uniform. Chains and franchises may differ from independent hotels in terms of flexibility, brand advantages, and exposure to market conditions, while country-level tourism dependence and regulation can further condition these relationships [N7-R3][N7-R2][N7-R4][N10]. The existing evidence is strongest for franchise-related effects and weakest for a comprehensive cross-country comparison of ownership forms, so conclusions should be cautious and context-dependent [N7-R3][N10].

## 2. Firm size effects and operational interpretation

The firm-size evidence indicates that size is an important operational determinant of hotel risk, but the interpretation varies by the variable used. The branch report notes that size, profitability, and debt are part of the stylized results in hotel default studies [N2-R1]. It also highlights that revenue, room count, and asset size are operationally meaningful measures: revenue reflects performance, room count reflects physical scale, and asset size reflects capital intensity [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R5].

The evidence does not support a simple “larger hotels are more resilient” conclusion. Instead, it suggests that larger hotels may have different risk profiles depending on context. The hotel default literature indicates that profitability and size can interact, implying that larger hotels may have more capacity to absorb debt or generate stable revenue, but they may also be more capital-intensive and thus more sensitive to cash flow shocks [N2-R1][N2-R4]. The survival-analysis hotel study supports this by showing that survival is influenced by size, location, executive management, and the business cycle, meaning size is part of a broader set of determinants rather than a standalone predictor [N4-F1].

Firm size also interacts with financial ratios and survival. The branch reports indicate that size can moderate the effect of leverage and profitability: larger hotels may experience different financing constraints or operational dynamics than smaller ones [N2-R1][N4-F1]. Overall, firm size should be treated as an important operational variable that interacts with financial ratios, but the exact mechanism differs by hotel and market context [N2-R1][N4-F1].

## 3. Country-level differences and structural context

The country-level evidence shows that European hotel risk patterns are shaped by tourism dependence, regulation, market structure, and national economic conditions. The branch report notes that tourism participation and overnight spending vary substantially across European countries, with some countries having much lower tourism participation than others [N6-F3]. It also highlights that tourism dependence and market concentration can make hotels more vulnerable to national tourism cycles and regulatory changes [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3].

The platformization and regulation evidence also shows that market concentration and regulatory interventions can shape the competitive environment for hotels [N3-R2][N3-R4]. The hotel-default literature likewise indicates that structural factors can condition hotel risk, alongside financial variables [N2-R1][N3-R5].

The branch reports do not provide a direct ranking of countries by default-risk intensity, but they do point to countries with stronger tourism dependence and market concentration as likely to have more volatile hotel risk. Germany, France, and the Netherlands appear to be major contributors to international tourism spending, while Romania, Greece, Bulgaria, Italy, and Portugal show much lower overnight spending abroad [N6-F3]. Spain is also highlighted as the top EU destination for international tourists, suggesting a highly concentrated and potentially more sensitive hotel market [N6-F3]. However, the provided evidence does not establish a direct link between tourism intensity and hotel default risk; it only shows that tourism is uneven and that structural factors differ across countries [N3-R1][N3-R3][N6-F3].

## 4. Cross-country heterogeneity: financial vs. structural factors

The branch reports suggest that cross-country heterogeneity is partly explained by structural factors rather than financial ratios alone. The hotel-default literature indicates that profitability and size are important, but the structural evidence shows that tourism dependence, regulation, and market structure can also explain differences in hotel risk [N2-R1][N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R2]. The tourism-disintermediation study also reports an econometric analysis of the hotel industry in 120 countries, emphasizing direct marketing and risk, and it implies that national regulatory and market structures can influence hotel risk through channels such as direct marketing and disintermediation [N3-R5].

In other words, the evidence supports a mixed picture: hotel default risk is shaped by both financial variables and structural variables. Financial ratios and firm size are important, but they operate within a broader context of tourism dependence, market structure, regulation, and national economic conditions [N2-R1][N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5]. That makes cross-country comparisons challenging because differences in national tourism systems and regulatory environments can condition the same financial variables differently [N6-F3][N3-R2][N3-R4].

## 5. Ownership/structure effects and heterogeneity

The ownership/structure evidence suggests that ownership form is an important source of heterogeneity in hotel default risk and survival, but the results are mixed. The franchise literature indicates that evidence on failure rates of franchised hotels versus independent hotels remains inconclusive, and that franchisors typically do not grant unlimited flexibility in operating decisions [N7-R3]. Another study shows that ownership form affects human resource practices in franchise systems, which is relevant because human capital can influence operational resilience and distress outcomes [N7-R2]. The franchise-and-expansion study also notes that franchisor internationalization decisions are positively related to franchise composition, suggesting that ownership structure can shape scale and market positioning [N7-R4].

The branch reports indicate that chains, franchises, and independent hotels may differ in terms of flexibility, brand advantages, and exposure to market conditions. Franchised hotels may face more standardized operating rules, which can reduce operational discretion but also provide brand and scale advantages [N7-R3][N7-R4]. Independent hotels may have more flexibility in pricing, marketing, and cost control, but they may also face higher exposure to local demand volatility and less access to brand capital [N7-R3]. The evidence does not establish a clear ranking of which ownership form is best in terms of survival, but it does suggest that ownership structure affects risk through different channels [N7-R2][N7-R3][N7-R4].

Ownership effects also interact with financial ratios and country context. The branch reports indicate that structural variables such as ownership, market concentration, and regulation can interact with financial ratios to shape survival prospects [N4-F1][N10]. In countries with high tourism dependence or concentrated hotel markets, ownership structure may be more important because hotels are more exposed to national tourism cycles and regulatory constraints [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R2]. In countries with more competitive or deregulated markets, independent hotels may have more room to adjust financially, whereas franchise networks may benefit from scale and brand strength [N3-R2][N3-R4]. Overall, ownership structure is a meaningful source of heterogeneity, but the direction of effect is not uniform [N7-R3][N10].

## 6. Methodological approach and cross-country comparability

The model-choice evidence shows that hotel risk analysis commonly uses survival analysis, logistic regression, and panel-data survival models, with survival analysis being especially prominent in hotel studies [N4-F1][N5-R2]. The multilevel survival tutorial describes frailty models and piecewise methods for multilevel survival data, showing that hotel risk analysis is increasingly moving toward more flexible survival models [N5-R3]. The Stata evidence also indicates that panel-data parametric survival models are available, which is relevant for cross-country studies that observe hotels over time [N5-R2].

Panel, fixed effects, and hazard models differ in interpretation. Panel models are useful when the same hotel is observed over time, allowing for time-specific and hotel-specific variation [N5-R2]. Fixed effects in survival analysis are often implemented through stratification, as the evidence explains that individual fixed effects in a Cox model are realized through the “strata” command [N5-R5]. Hazard models, such as the Cox proportional hazards model, estimate the instantaneous risk of an event occurring at each time point, conditional on surviving up to that point [N5-R4]. The key difference is that hazard models directly estimate risk dynamics, while fixed effects or panel methods control for unobserved heterogeneity [N5-R2][N5-R5].

The branch reports also highlight limitations of cross-country comparisons. First, hotel studies often use survival analysis, which can be sensitive to the length of the observation period and the timing of events [N4-F1]. Second, the survival-analysis hotel study is country-specific to Spain, which means its results are not directly generalizable to other European countries without replication [N4-F1]. Third, structural factors such as tourism dependence and market structure vary across countries, making direct comparisons difficult [N3-R1][N3-R3]. Finally, the evidence indicates that cross-country comparability is constrained by differences in data sources, registration schemes, and national accounting practices, especially for hotel and tourism data [N6-F3].

To address these limitations, the branch reports suggest three main approaches: use country-level controls and interaction terms to allow for heterogeneous effects, use panel or fixed-effects models to control for unobserved heterogeneity, and rely on comparable data sources such as Eurostat and national statistics where possible [N4-F1][N5-R2][N5-R5][N6-F3]. Overall, the evidence supports survival analysis as the most appropriate method for hotel risk studies, but cross-country comparisons require careful methodological safeguards and explicit attention to structural differences [N4-F1][N5-R2][N6-F3].

## 7. Integrated conclusion

Taken together, the branch reports support the following integrated conclusion:

- **Financial ratios** are the most consistent predictors of hotel default risk and survival, with liquidity, leverage, profitability, and cash flow being the most frequently used indicators [N1-R4][N2-R1][N4-F1][N1-R5].
- **Firm size** is an important operational determinant, but it does not provide a universal “resilience” effect: larger hotels may be more or less risky depending on context, and size interacts with financial ratios and survival [N2-R1][N2-R4][N4-F1].
- **Country-level differences** matter because tourism dependence, regulation, and market structure shape hotel risk differently across European countries [N6-F3][N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R2].
- **Ownership structure** adds important heterogeneity: chains, franchises, and independent hotels may differ in flexibility, brand advantages, and exposure to market conditions, and these effects can interact with financial ratios and country context [N7-R3][N7-R2][N7-R4][N10].
- **Methodological choices** matter for cross-country comparability: survival analysis is standard, but panel and fixed-effects approaches help control for heterogeneity, while structural differences across countries make direct comparisons difficult [N4-F1][N5-R2][N5-R5][N6-F3].

In short, hotel default risk and survival are not determined by any single factor. They depend on a combination of **financial health**, **operational scale**, **ownership form**, and **country-specific structural conditions**. The strongest evidence is that hotels with better liquidity and stronger profitability are more likely to survive, while high leverage and poor cash flow increase default risk [N1-R4][N2-R1]. At the same time, hotels in countries with stronger tourism dependence or concentrated markets face different risk dynamics, and ownership structure can amplify or moderate these effects [N6-F3][N3-R1][N10].

The branch reports suggest that cross-country heterogeneity is partly explained by structural factors rather than financial ratios alone. The branch reports indicate that chains, franchises, and independent hotels may differ in terms of flexibility, brand advantages, and exposure to market conditions. Overall, ownership structure is a meaningful source of heterogeneity, but the direction of effect is not uniform [N7-R3][N10].

## 6. Methodological approach and cross-country comparability

The model-choice evidence shows that hotel risk analysis commonly uses survival analysis, logistic regression, and panel-data survival models, with survival analysis being especially prominent in hotel studies [N4-F1][N5-R2]. The multilevel survival tutorial describes frailty models and piecewise methods for multilevel survival data, showing that hotel risk analysis is increasingly moving toward more flexible survival models [N5-R3]. The Stata evidence also indicates that panel-data parametric survival models are available, which is relevant for cross-country studies that observe hotels over time [N5-R2].

Panel, fixed effects, and hazard models differ in interpretation. Panel models are useful when the same hotel is observed over time, allowing for time-specific and hotel-specific variation [N5-R2]. Fixed effects in survival analysis are often implemented through stratification, as the evidence explains that individual fixed effects in a Cox model are realized through the “strata” command [N5-R5]. Hazard models, such as the Cox proportional hazards model, estimate the instantaneous risk of an event occurring at each time point, conditional on surviving up to that point [N5-R4]. The key difference is that hazard models directly estimate risk dynamics, while fixed effects or panel methods control for unobserved heterogeneity [N5-R2][N5-R5].

The branch reports also highlight limitations of cross-country comparisons. First, hotel studies often use survival analysis, which can be sensitive to the length of the observation period and the timing of events [N4-F1]. Second, the survival-analysis hotel study is country-specific to Spain, which means its results are not directly generalizable to other European countries without replication [N4-F1]. Third, structural factors such as tourism dependence and market structure vary across countries, making direct comparisons difficult [N3-R1][N3-R3]. Finally, the evidence indicates that cross-country comparability is constrained by differences in data sources, registration schemes, and national accounting practices, especially for hotel and tourism data [N6-F3].

To address these limitations, the branch reports suggest three main approaches: use country-level controls and interaction terms to allow for heterogeneous effects, use panel or fixed-effects models to control for unobserved heterogeneity, and rely on comparable data sources such as Eurostat and national statistics where possible [N4-F1][N5-R2][N5-R5][N6-F3]. Overall, the evidence supports survival analysis as the most appropriate method for hotel risk studies, but cross-country comparisons require careful methodological safeguards and explicit attention to structural differences [N4-F1][N5-R2][N6-F3].

## 7. Integrated conclusion

Taken together, the branch reports support the following integrated conclusion:

- **Financial ratios** are the most consistent predictors of hotel default risk and survival, with liquidity, leverage, profitability, and cash flow being the most frequently used indicators [N1-R4][N2-R1][N4-F1][N1-R5].
- **Firm size** is an important operational determinant, but it does not provide a universal “resilience” effect: larger hotels may be more or less risky depending on context, and size interacts with financial ratios and survival [N2-R1][N2-R4][N4-F1].
- **Country-level differences** matter because tourism dependence, regulation, and market structure shape hotel risk differently across European countries [N6-F3][N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R2].
- **Ownership structure** adds important heterogeneity: chains, franchises, and independent hotels may differ in flexibility, brand advantages, and exposure to market conditions, and these effects can interact with financial ratios and country context [N7-R3][N7-R2][N7-R4][N10].
- **Methodological choices** matter for cross-country comparability: survival analysis is standard, but panel and fixed-effects approaches help control for heterogeneity, while structural differences across countries make direct comparisons difficult [N4-F1][N5-R2][N5-R5][N6-F3].

In short, hotel default risk and survival are not determined by any single factor. They depend on a combination of **financial health**, **operational scale**, **ownership form**, and **country-specific structural conditions**. The strongest evidence is that hotels with better liquidity and stronger profitability are more likely to survive, while high leverage and poor cash flow increase default risk [N1-R4][N2-R1]. The tourism-led-growth paper argues that southern European economies increasingly exploit comparative advantage in tourism, which implies that tourism dependence can be both an opportunity and a vulnerability [N3-R3]. The platformization and regulation evidence also shows that market concentration and regulatory interventions can shape the competitive environment for hotels [N3-R2][N3-R4]. The hotel-default literature likewise indicates that structural factors can condition hotel risk, alongside financial variables [N2-R1][N3-R5].

The branch reports do not provide a direct ranking of countries by default-risk intensity, but they do point to countries with stronger tourism dependence and market concentration as likely to have more volatile hotel risk. Germany, France, and the Netherlands appear to be major contributors to international tourism spending, while Romania, Greece, Bulgaria, Italy, and Portugal show much lower overnight spending abroad [N6-F3]. Spain is also highlighted as the top EU destination for international tourists, suggesting a highly concentrated and potentially more sensitive hotel market [N6-F3]. However, the provided evidence does not establish a direct link between tourism intensity and hotel default risk; it only shows that tourism is uneven and that structural factors differ across countries [N3-R1][N3-R3][N6-F3].

## 4. Cross-country heterogeneity: financial vs. structural factors

The branch reports suggest that cross-country heterogeneity is partly explained by structural factors rather than financial ratios alone. The hotel-default literature indicates that profitability and size are important, but the structural evidence shows that tourism dependence, regulation, and market structure can also explain differences in hotel risk [N2-R1][N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R2]. The tourism-disintermediation study also reports an econometric analysis of the hotel industry in 120 countries, emphasizing direct marketing and risk, and it implies that national regulatory and market structures can influence hotel risk through channels such as direct marketing and disintermediation [N3-R5].

In other words, the evidence supports a mixed picture: hotel default risk is shaped by both financial variables and structural variables. Financial ratios and firm size are important, but they operate within a broader context of tourism dependence, market structure, regulation, and national economic conditions [N2-R1][N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5]. That makes cross-country comparisons challenging because differences in national tourism systems and regulatory environments can condition the same financial variables differently [N6-F3][N3-R2][N3-R4].

## 5. Ownership/structure effects and heterogeneity

The ownership/structure evidence suggests that ownership form is an important source of heterogeneity in hotel default risk and survival, but the results are mixed. The franchise literature indicates that evidence on failure rates of franchised hotels versus independent hotels remains inconclusive, and that franchisors typically do not grant unlimited flexibility in operating decisions [N7-R3]. Another study shows that ownership form affects human resource practices in franchise systems, which is relevant because human capital can influence operational resilience and distress outcomes [N7-R2]. The franchise-and-expansion study also notes that franchisor internationalization decisions are positively related to franchise composition, suggesting that ownership structure can shape scale and market positioning [N7-R4].

The branch reports indicate that chains, franchises, and independent hotels may differ in terms of flexibility, brand advantages, and exposure to market conditions. Franchised hotels may face more standardized operating rules, which can reduce operational discretion but also provide brand and scale advantages [N7-R3][N7-R4]. Independent hotels may have more flexibility in pricing, marketing, and cost control, but they may also face higher exposure to local demand volatility and less access to brand capital [N7-R3]. The evidence does not establish a clear ranking of which ownership form is best in terms of survival, but it does suggest that ownership structure affects risk through different channels [N7-R2][N7-R3][N7-R4].

Ownership effects also interact with financial ratios and country context. The branch reports indicate that structural variables such as ownership, market concentration, and regulation can interact with financial ratios to shape survival prospects [N4-F1][N10]. In countries with high tourism dependence or concentrated hotel markets, ownership structure may be more important because hotels are more exposed to national tourism cycles and regulatory constraints [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R2]. In countries with more competitive or deregulated markets, independent hotels may have more room to adjust financially, whereas franchise networks may benefit from scale and brand strength [N3-R2][N3-R4]. Overall, ownership structure is a meaningful source of heterogeneity, but the direction of effect is not uniform [N7-R3][N10].

## 6. Methodological approach and cross-country comparability

The model-choice evidence shows that hotel risk analysis commonly uses survival analysis, logistic regression, and panel-data survival models, with survival analysis being especially prominent in hotel studies [N4-F1][N5-R2]. The multilevel survival tutorial describes frailty models and piecewise methods for multilevel survival data, showing that hotel risk analysis is increasingly moving toward more flexible survival models [N5-R3]. The Stata evidence also indicates that panel-data parametric survival models are available, which is relevant for cross-country studies that observe hotels over time [N5-R2].

Panel, fixed effects, and hazard models differ in interpretation. Panel models are useful when the same hotel is observed over time, allowing for time-specific and hotel-specific variation [N5-R2]. Fixed effects in survival analysis are often implemented through stratification, as the evidence explains that individual fixed effects in a Cox model are realized through the “strata” command [N5-R5]. Hazard models, such as the Cox proportional hazards model, estimate the instantaneous risk of an event occurring at each time point, conditional on surviving up to that point [N5-R4]. The key difference is that hazard models directly estimate risk dynamics, while fixed effects or panel methods control for unobserved heterogeneity [N5-R2][N5-R5].

The branch reports also highlight limitations of cross-country comparisons. First, hotel studies often use survival analysis, which can be sensitive to the length of the observation period and the timing of events [N4-F1]. Second, the survival-analysis hotel study is country-specific to Spain, which means its results are not directly generalizable to other European countries without replication [N4-F1]. Third, structural factors such as tourism dependence and market structure vary across countries, making direct comparisons difficult [N3-R1][N3-R3]. Finally, the evidence indicates that cross-country comparability is constrained by differences in data sources, registration schemes, and national accounting practices, especially for hotel and tourism data [N6-F3].

To address these limitations, the branch reports suggest three main approaches: use country-level controls and interaction terms to allow for heterogeneous effects, use panel or fixed-effects models to control for unobserved heterogeneity, and rely on comparable data sources such as Eurostat and national statistics where possible [N4-F1][N5-R2][N5-R5][N6-F3]. Overall, the evidence supports survival analysis as the most appropriate method for hotel risk studies, but cross-country comparisons require careful methodological safeguards and explicit attention to structural differences [N4-F1][N5-R2][N6-F3].

## 7. Integrated conclusion

Taken together, the branch reports support the following integrated conclusion:

- **Financial ratios** are the most consistent predictors of hotel default risk and survival, with liquidity, leverage, profitability, and cash flow being the most frequently used indicators [N1-R4][N2-R1][N4-F1][N1-R5].
- **Firm size** is an important operational determinant, but it does not provide a universal “resilience” effect: larger hotels may be more or less risky depending on context, and size interacts with financial ratios and survival [N2-R1][N2-R4][N4-F1].
- **Country-level differences** matter because tourism dependence, regulation, and market structure shape hotel risk differently across European countries [N6-F3][N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R2].
- **Ownership structure** adds important heterogeneity: chains, franchises, and independent hotels may differ in flexibility, brand advantages, and exposure to market conditions, and these effects can interact with financial ratios and country context [N7-R3][N7-R2][N7-R4][N10].
- **Methodological choices** matter for cross-country comparability: survival analysis is standard, but panel and fixed-effects approaches help control for heterogeneity, while structural differences across countries make direct comparisons difficult [N4-F1][N5-R2][N5-R5][N6-F3].

In short, hotel default risk and survival are not determined by any single factor. They depend on a combination of **financial health**, **operational scale**, **ownership form**, and **country-specific structural conditions**. The strongest evidence is that hotels with better liquidity and stronger profitability are more likely to survive, while high leverage and poor cash flow increase default risk [N1-R4][N2-R1]. At the same time, hotels in countries with stronger tourism dependence or concentrated markets face different risk dynamics, and ownership structure can amplify or moderate these effects [N6-F3][N3-R1][N10].
